title: Transpose Matrix
description: Brute force to optimized: building rows via repeated appends versus pre-allocating the known final shape and assigning directly.

blocks.text: Given a 2D integer array matrix, return its TRANSPOSE: the matrix formed by flipping matrix over its main diagonal, so that row and column indices of every element are swapped.

blocks.caption: Every element at [i][j] moves to [j][i] in the transposed result

blocks.text: Given a matrix with rows rows and cols columns, produce its transpose: a new matrix with cols rows and rows columns, where the element at row i, column j in the original becomes the element at row j, column i in the result.

blocks.title: Analogy: Flipping a Grid of Seats Over Its Diagonal
blocks.text: Like relabeling a rectangular grid of theater seats by swapping "row number" and "seat number" for every seat, turning a grid of R rows and C seats-per-row into a grid of C rows and R seats-per-row, with each seat's occupant carried over to its new, swapped position.

blocks.caption: Swapping every element's row and column index also swaps the matrix's overall shape

blocks.content: {"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["Row 0 [1,2,3] becomes column 0 of the result; row 1 [4,5,6] becomes column 1; row 2 [7,8,9] becomes column 2","Result: [[1,4,7],[2,5,8],[3,6,9]]","Every element matrix[i][j] moves to result[j][i]"],["Answer","[[1,4,7],[2,5,8],[3,6,9]]","This is the transpose of the original 3x3 matrix"]]}

{"headers":["Step","Result","Why"],"rows":[["The 2x3 input becomes a 3x2 output: row 0 [1,2,3] becomes column 0; row 1 [4,5,6] becomes column 1","Result: [[1,4],[2,5],[3,6]]","The output shape is always the input's shape with rows and columns swapped"],["Answer","[[1,4],[2,5],[3,6]]","This is the transpose of the original 2x3 matrix, now shaped 3x2"]]}

blocks.text: Before building the result row by row with dynamic appends, notice that the exact final shape is already known upfront, letting the result be pre-allocated and filled directly.

blocks.title: Building the Intuition
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The transpose of a matrix with rows rows and cols columns always has exactly cols rows and rows columns, a shape known immediately from the input's dimensions.

Observation 2: Every single element matrix[i][j] has one, and only one, destination in the result: position [j][i]. There's no ambiguity or need to search for where an element belongs.

Observation 3: Since the destination for every element is known directly from its own indices, the result can be pre-allocated to its exact final size, and every element can be placed directly, with no dynamic resizing or intermediate rebuilding needed at all.

Recognizing that the exact output shape and every element's destination are both known in advance (unlike problems requiring conditional logic to decide where something belongs) is what makes a single direct-assignment pass sufficient.
This is a direct index-mapping problem: every element's destination is a simple, known formula (swap the two indices), with no decision-making required at all.
Build each new row of the result by appending elements one at a time, iterating column-major over the original matrix.

items: For every column j of the original matrix, build a new row by appending matrix[i][j] for every row i, in order.
Collect these new rows together to form the transposed matrix.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: Each new row is built by appending elements one at a time, which works correctly but repeatedly resizes the underlying row storage as it grows.
The outer loop iterates over columns first, since each output row corresponds to one column of the original matrix.
result naturally ends up with the correct final shape once every row has been fully built and collected.

blocks.text: Every element is visited and placed correctly, so the transpose is always produced accurately.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows * cols), visiting every element exactly once, though repeated appends can carry extra amortized overhead from dynamic array resizing.
Space: O(rows * cols) for the output matrix, which is unavoidable since the output has just as many elements as the input.

Limitation: building each row via repeated appends does unnecessary extra work managing dynamic resizing, when the exact final size of every row is already known in advance and could be allocated directly.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text: The brute force repeatedly appends to grow each row of the result, incurring avoidable resizing overhead. Instead, since the final shape (cols rows, each of length rows) is known immediately from the input's dimensions, pre-allocate the result matrix to that exact size upfront. Then, in a single pass over every (i, j) position in the original matrix, directly assign result[j][i] = matrix[i][j], with no resizing or rebuilding needed at all.
Pre-allocate a result matrix of size cols by rows. For every position (i, j) in the original matrix, directly assign matrix[i][j] to result[j][i].
Pre-allocate the exact final shape, then directly assign every element to its transposed position.

blocks.title: Final result
blocks.text: result = [[1,4,7],[2,5,8],[3,6,9]], matching the expected transpose exactly.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(rows * cols), visiting every element exactly once with no resizing overhead.
Space: O(rows * cols) for the output matrix, which is unavoidable for a non-square matrix (since a differently-shaped result must always be produced).

Every element's destination in the transpose is determined entirely by its own (i, j) position, via the simple formula (j, i), with no dependency on any other element or any decision-making. Pre-allocating the exact final shape and assigning directly avoids all the incidental overhead of building the result incrementally.

No intermediate lists, dynamic appends, or resizing operations are needed anywhere in this version.

blocks.text: When both the exact output shape and every element's exact destination are known upfront, pre-allocating the result and assigning directly avoids all incidental overhead from dynamic data structure growth.

items: Confusing rows and columns when allocating the result's shape, producing a result with the wrong dimensions.

Attempting an in-place transpose on a non-square matrix, which is fundamentally impossible since the physical shape itself changes (a rows-by-cols storage block cannot become cols-by-rows without reallocation when rows != cols).
Off-by-one or swapped-index errors when writing matrix[i][j] to result[j][i] (writing to result[i][j] instead, for example).

items: Mention the in-place swap trick for SQUARE matrices as a space-saving follow-up, while being clear that it fundamentally cannot apply to non-square matrices, since interviewers often probe this exact distinction.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text: "Transpose a matrix" points toward a direct index-swap mapping (result[j][i] = matrix[i][j]), pre-allocating the known cols-by-rows output shape upfront.

items: How would you transpose a SQUARE matrix in-place, using no extra space? Swap matrix[i][j] with matrix[j][i] for every pair where i < j, leaving the diagonal (i == j) untouched.

How would this extend to a 3D array (a "cube" of values)? Transposing higher-dimensional arrays generalizes to permuting axis indices, though the specific axes being swapped would need to be defined explicitly.
What if the matrix were extremely wide or tall (very unbalanced dimensions)? The same technique applies unchanged; time and space remain O(rows * cols) regardless of the aspect ratio.

A foundational matrix-manipulation building block, whose direct index-swap idea reappears (often combined with additional constraints) in problems like Rotate Image, which builds on transpose-then-reverse as one common rotation technique.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text:
Brute force: O(rows * cols) amortized time, O(rows * cols) space.
Optimized (pre-allocate, direct assignment): O(rows * cols) time, O(rows * cols) space.

items: Pattern: Direct index-swap mapping over a pre-allocated result matrix
Core Idea: Every element matrix[i][j] has exactly one destination, result[j][i]; pre-allocating the known final shape avoids all incidental overhead
Time: O(rows * cols)
Space: O(rows * cols) (O(1) extra possible in-place, but only for square matrices)
Most Important Observation: The transpose's exact output shape and every element's destination are both known immediately from the input's dimensions
Interview Difficulty: Easy
One-line memory trick: result[j][i] = matrix[i][j]
